newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Cold, rain return to western Europe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cold, rain return to western Europe.

text.p: Cold, wet weather returned to western Europe over the weekend and Monday, and more is predicted.

Rain did much to ease farmers' fears over the effects of a long dry spell on developing grains and sugar beet but the cold which came with the rain over the weekend and on Monday is causing new worries.
Unsettled weather spoilt Britain's bank holiday on Monday for many and pushed up energy demand as heating was switched back on.

Farming experts welcomed the rain, which had enabled developing crops to forge ahead, but now there were fears that forecast frost may damage crops, while water settling on the surface of dried out ground could make planting difficult in places.
And the rain has not been enough to replenish low water stocks and make sufficient supplies available for irrigation in many areas.
In Britain, the weekend weather led to a large volume of natural gas purchased on the flexibility mechanism, which is designed to cope with demand swings and keep the gas pipeline system in balance.
In France, the rain eased concerns over the grain crop but will do little to address long-term water problems after months of dry weather, government experts and farmers said on Monday.

"The rain made a dent in the drought situation and gave relief to the crops," a weather specialist at the environment ministry said. But the amount of rainfall was not enough to replenish water tables below the soil's surface.
National weather serice Meteo France measured the weekend's rainfall at 10-20 mm.
Forecasters expect cooler temperatures and some rainfall to last until at least mid-week.
The rain however helped the growth of spring crops and in the southwest allowed farmers to get on with maize sowings.
There is a possibility that excessive rain on dry soil could mean water staying on the surface and make field work difficult for farmers trying to get on with sowing.
The EU has pushed back the deadline for farmers to declare maize and other late grain sowings by two weeks because of the drought, the French agriculture ministry said on Tuesday.
The APCA farm lobby said spring crops may escape unscathed but there were worries over the fate of winter grains.
"The rain helped winter grain but will not make up for ground lost earlier," an official there said.
"If precipitation returns to normal levels we can hope yields will be in line with an average year," he said.
The spring grain crop is dominated by maize and about 40 percent of French barley is grown from spring varieties. But nearly all the country's wheat grows through the winter.

Weather experts say underground water resources are 25 percent below normal across three quarters of the French countryside. In about half the country, the deficit measured against the seasonal average has reached 50 percent.
Weekend rain over southern and eastern England eased some of the concerns over parched British crops, but as the weather turned colder, frost was becoming an increasing fear for farmers.

In the 24 hours to 0600 GMT on Tuesday rainfall in the important cereals producing areas of eastern England ranged from 7-8 millimetres up to 10-12 millimetres in places, a spokesman for the London Weather Centre said.

But the immediate worry for farmers is the frost forecast for Tuesday evening in many areas. Some barley crops, which are well forward, could be especially at risk, according to an expert at agricultural consultants ADAS.
The rain helped most crops get back to normal, he said. "The rain has darkened everything up," he said, as crops absorb the moisture and turn greener.
"Everything should start coming through a storm now, providing this frost doesn't do too much damage," he said.
The rain was exactly what was needed. "When it rained last week we said we needed this every ten days or so, and the weather has obliged," the ADAS expert said.
Intermittent showers and cool weather are likely to continue at least until the weekend, forecasters said.

But the showers are not going to be enough to solve the long term irrigation problems of farmers, or the supply worries of domestic water providers. "You'd have to be looking at a Noah's Ark situation for it to make any difference," one water industry source said.
According to the independent forecaster Weather Services Corp, drought-breaking rains have developed in western Europe including northern Spain, France, the Benelux countries and Britain.

It forecast more rain in western Europe for Tuesday and a few light showers in the more eastern areas with this pattern continuing on Wednesday. Rainfall will be significant this week in the west, breaking the drought, while the weather is forecast mild and drier in the east, especially the Southeast, WSC said.
In its three-to-five day forecast, WSC said Western Europe will have periods of rain and fog on Thursday to Friday and lingering showers on Saturday, mostly in the north. It will be cool.

Germany and Central Europe will also be showery and cool while Mediterranean Europe will have showers in western and central areas on Thursday, and in eastern areas on Saturday, with temperatures cooling west to east. From Saturday it will be drier as temperatures return to near normal.

In eastern Europe showers and thunderstorms will develop from west to east during Thursday with temperatures still above normal. There will be a chance of rain during Friday with temperatures turning cooler. Temperatures will be near to below normal on Saturday with showers likely.
